meta_desc_nationwide: National statistics from MEXT and the guidance revised in August 2026, showing how school consolidation is proceeding across Japan and what standards the national government sets.
meta_title_nationwide: School Reorganization Nationwide – Komaki East (Shinooka) School Reorganization Plan
nationwide_p: School reorganization is not happening only in eastern Komaki. By placing the national standards and nationwide statistics side by side, this page shows where this plan sits.
nationwide_ref_box:
Sources and references (all from MEXT)
  • Appropriate size and placement of public elementary and junior high schools
  • Notice on the revision of the guidance (5 August 2026)
  • Survey on the use of closed school facilities (FY2024)
  • School Basic Survey (FY2025)
This page is background information about the national situation. For facts about the eastern Komaki plan itself, see the other pages, which are based on the city's official information. This is an unofficial citizen-run site, not a website of Komaki City.
nationwide_row1_komaki: On the current trend, every elementary school and Shinooka JHS would have just one class per grade by 2033.
nationwide_row1_national: 12 to 18 classes is the standard for elementary and junior high schools; 18 to 27 for compulsory education schools.
nationwide_row2_komaki: School buses for elementary pupils commuting 2 km or more, fully funded by the city (free of charge).
nationwide_row2_national: Roughly within 4 km for elementary and 6 km for junior high (the condition for national subsidy).
nationwide_row3_komaki: Stops and timetable to be set in the “School Bus Use Guidelines” and shown at the briefing for eligible families.
nationwide_row3_national: Where transport is used, roughly one hour or less is the rough guideline.
nationwide_s1_lead: School consolidation driven by the falling birthrate has continued across Japan for decades. These are the nationwide closure figures from MEXT surveys.
nationwide_s1_note: The number of public elementary and junior high schools fell by about 2,000 in roughly ten years, and the number of pupils by about 850,000.
nationwide_s2_h: What the National Standards Say<small>National Standards</small>
nationwide_s2_lead: The national government sets guideline figures for school size and commuting conditions. All of them are flexible — "unless there are special circumstances" — and each municipality decides for itself what to actually do.
nationwide_s2_note: The national figures come from Articles 41, 49 and 79-3 of the Enforcement Regulations of the School Education Act, and Article 4 of the Enforcement Order of the Act on National Treasury Subsidies for School Facilities. For Komaki's own commuting plan, see the School Bus page.
nationwide_s3_basic:
• Improving educational conditions for children is the centre of any review.
  • Each municipality decides for itself.
  • Whether schools are merged or kept, the benefits must be used and the drawbacks minimized.
nationwide_s3_bus: On school buses: Because the shortage of drivers is affecting local public transport as a whole, the revision states that municipalities considering buses should work with the mayor's departments to secure transport for the area as a whole.
nationwide_s3_c1_p: Rather than looking only within its own boundaries, a municipality should consider the wider area including neighbouring municipalities. Schools jointly established by several municipalities are given as an example.
nationwide_s3_c2_p: Not only the board of education but the mayor's departments too should treat this as a question about the area's future, considered together with transport provision and town planning.
nationwide_s3_c3_p: The text is updated for the revised curriculum guidelines and for learning that assumes one device per pupil, including linking small schools to each other online.
nationwide_s3_h: August 2026: National Guidance Revised for the First Time in Ten Years<small>Revised Guidance</small>
nationwide_s3_lead: MEXT has revised, for the first time in ten years, the guidance municipalities use when reviewing school size and placement. The revision has three main points.
nationwide_s3_quote: New wording on building consensus: The revision adds the importance of "careful, dialogue-based discussion" and of setting "a timeline that does not keep postponing a conclusion." It states that the process matters — not merely asking whether to merge, but having everyone involved discuss what a school is for and how they want children to grow.
nationwide_s4_h: School Size and Pupil Numbers Nationwide<small>Scale and Numbers</small>
nationwide_s4_lead: The situation troubling eastern Komaki — close to one class per grade — is happening at many schools across Japan.
nationwide_s4_list:
• About 40% of public elementary schools and about 50% of public junior high schools have fewer than 12 classes.
  • About 16% of municipalities are down to a single elementary school and a single junior high school — some 60 more than a decade ago.
  • Elementary pupils number 5,812,000 and junior high students 3,105,000, both record lows (as of 1 May 2025).
nationwide_s4_note: Sources: MEXT "Outline of the Revised Guidance" (August 2026) and the FY2025 School Basic Survey (final figures).
nationwide_s5_h: The Combined Elementary–Junior High Option<small>Compulsory Education Schools</small>
nationwide_s5_link: See what is being considered for Phase 2 →
nationwide_s5_p: Under the eastern Komaki plan, a second phase merging down to one elementary and one junior high school with combined elementary–junior high education is also being considered. Nationwide there were 232 public compulsory education schools — a single school covering both levels — in FY2024, with 75,828 pupils; enrolment reached a record 87,000 in FY2025. The statutory standard size is 18 to 27 classes.
nationwide_source_intro: Sources: Every figure and standard on this page comes from materials published by MEXT (Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology). For the Komaki plan itself, see Plan Overview.

nationwide_terms: <dt>Appropriate size and placement</dt><dd>Reviewing the number of classes and the location of schools from the standpoint of children's educational conditions. The state issues guidance; each municipality decides.</dd><dt>Compulsory education school</dt><dd>A single school covering elementary and junior high, able to run one nine-year curriculum.</dd><dt>One-and-one municipality</dt><dd>A municipality left with just one elementary and one junior high school. About 16% of municipalities are in this position.</dd><dt>Reuse of closed schools</dt><dd>Putting a disused school building or gymnasium to another use. 74.4% of the closed schools still standing are in use.</dd>
